verdict: Only one item changes what you tell patients, and it's a null result.
caveat: Sample edition built from the format test. All three items were read from abstracts or synopses, and sources are not yet verified.

items.title: Antibiotics don't help chronic LBP with disc herniation
items.impact_line: If a patient asks about antibiotics for Modic changes: a placebo-controlled trial of 170 found no benefit at 12 months and more side effects.
items.summary: Amoxicillin-clavulanate for 90 days gave no pain benefit over placebo at 12 months. Patients with Modic changes did no better. Adverse events were more common on the antibiotic.

pico.p: Adults with chronic LBP and disc herniation, n = 170

key_numbers.label: adjusted pain difference, 0–10 scale (95% CI -0.58 to 0.70)

items.limits: One trial. Numbers come from synopses; check the full text before quoting them to a referrer.

full_text.why: Everything above comes from synopses, so subgroup and harms detail is thin.

items.title: Intradiscal hydrogel vs sham: primary outcome missed
items.impact_line: Nothing to change. If a patient raises disc implants, the honest answer is early sham-controlled data with no clear primary-outcome win.
items.summary: A percutaneous hydrogel implant did not clearly beat sham on the primary outcome. A secondary global-improvement measure favoured treatment, but secondary outcomes in a small trial are hypothesis-generating at best.
items.limits: Small, abstract only, and a secondary outcome carries the headline.

full_text.why: Know-don't-act item; the abstract is enough for now.

items.title: Conservative care helps early; by 12 months the gap fades
items.impact_line: Frame conservative care as helping most in the first few months, and set expectations that differences between treatments shrink by 12 months.
items.summary: Pools 551 trials and 71,126 patients with chronic non-specific LBP. Short-term benefits appear for exercise, manual therapy, acupuncture, massage, electrotherapy and multidisciplinary care; by 12 months they are hard to find.
items.limits: Very low certainty evidence. Journal not confirmed; read via a summary page.

measure_of_week.name: H:Q ratio
measure_of_week.bottom_line: Use it to track an imbalance over time in the same athlete. Don't use it alone to call someone high risk.
measure_of_week.what_it_measures: Hamstring strength relative to quadriceps, usually from isokinetic peak torque.

numbers.value: Very limited evidence that any H:Q ratio independently predicts hamstring or ACL injury

numbers.population: Not stated in the source checked

measure_of_week.when_to_use: Return-to-sport and in-season monitoring, alongside absolute strength and other modifiable factors.
pitfalls: Ratios change with test velocity. Compare like with like.
A good ratio can hide two weak muscles. Check absolute torque too.
Devices and gravity correction differ. Retest on the same setup.
